extracted.intended_audience: writers (beginner to intermediate) creating flash fiction of 1,000 words or less; entrants in NYC Midnight-style contests
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing self-contained flash fiction pieces (≤1,000 words) that have a complete narrative arc, balanced character and plot, and are submission-ready for contests and literary magazines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flash fiction length and self-contained arc
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash fiction is a story of a thousand words or less and is self-contained rather than an excerpt from a longer piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each piece should have a polished narrative arc (beginning, middle, end) and feel whole without requiring outside context or backstory. NYC Midnight and many literary magazines define flash fiction as ≤1,000 words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete narrative arc despite brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Even with limited space, flash fiction must capture a complete narrative arc with a beginning, middle, and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The story should not be merely a snapshot or gesture; it should present a change for characters and move them into a changed state by the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of character and plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Good flash fiction balances focus on character and focus on plot; it isn’t just plot or just character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide plot points that a character we care about moves through. Ensure actions reveal character and that character choices drive plot progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as change and causal build
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the series of points that move a story from beginning to end and is defined by change for the characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot points should build on and inform one another; a streamlined, focused plot takes a character through a growth arc (for better or worse). Avoid disconnected bullet-point events that don’t cause or inform later events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot points must inform one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Each plot point should build on previous points so the reader understands why events matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use connective cause-and-effect so motivations and outcomes feel earned (example: the June class/date/watermelon example shows how building events create investment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character through action and reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be developed by what they do and how they respond, not by excess physical description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask how each action aligns with the personality you’ve crafted. Use behavior and choices to reveal character rather than listing physical traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit narrative POVs
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the number of narrative viewpoints in a flash piece; one POV is generally best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple viewpoints are difficult in limited space; if used, consider limiting to two and be extremely judicious with word choice so personalities remain distinct and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fewer characters / limit named characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the cast small—generally as few characters as possible, especially named ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only name characters who have bearing on the plot. Too many names split reader attention and dilute focus; background characters can remain unnamed unless essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single focus / contain the story
rubrics_metrics.description: A flash story should be contained to one single focus and limited scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose one facet you can do justice to in ~1,000 words and explore it in depth rather than attempting many threads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep it simple / avoid complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity serves thousand-word stories better than complicated plots or many threads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing, remove complicated directions or secondary strands that do not serve the core narrative; avoid writing a rushed summary rather than a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtract rather than add (kill your darlings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize cutting extraneous material over adding more to solve problems in a short piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move removed segments to a separate document if needed; ask what can be omitted while preserving core plot and character growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid or minimize subplots
rubrics_metrics.description: Subplots are usually unrewarding in flash fiction and can distract from the main arc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you include a subplot, ensure it never comes at the expense of the key narrative arc and that pacing of the main plot remains dominant. Novice writers are advised to shave subplots away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be judicious with backstory
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid infodumping; include only backstory elements that directly drive the story forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only include context essential to the plot or character motivation. If backstory doesn’t inform current stakes or actions, cut it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a full first draft without self-editing
rubrics_metrics.description: During the first draft, focus on getting the story down and do not self-edit heavily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep side stories and backstories to a minimum in the first pass; allow surprises and unanticipated directions to emerge, then trim in subsequent passes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trim using focused scene-evaluation questions
rubrics_metrics.description: On revision, evaluate each scene/beat by asking specific questions about its contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: How does this scene serve the arc? How does it push my characters to grow? How does it push the story forward? Does the setting challenge the characters? Omit or rework scenes that fail to answer satisfactorily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep descriptions relevant and integrated
rubrics_metrics.description: Use description sparingly and weave setting/physical detail into action rather than standalone paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infuse setting via actions (characters walking/buying/doing) so description serves plot or character. Avoid lengthy descriptive paragraphs that halt momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show physical details through interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical descriptions should be secondary to action and reveal character when interacted with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a physical detail is important, show how characters interact with it rather than merely observing it; this yields more insight with fewer words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dialogue to economize and reveal character
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue provides breathing room and can convey character quickly in fewer words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor speech for each character; maintain consistent voice differences. Let dialogue accomplish characterization and plot efficiently instead of exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize dialogue tags; use action beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep dialogue tags to a minimum and use actions to indicate speakers where clarity allows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it's clear who is speaking, omit tags. Replace 'John said shrilly' with an action beat (e.g., '“I’m going to bed.” John slammed the door.') when that action conveys emotion and identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get in late and get out early in scenes and dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin scenes and conversations as late as possible and end them early to maintain momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid showing the lead-up to conversation; start near the meat of the exchange and cut off before unnecessary trailing beats to keep readers engaged and conserve words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow formatting and submission guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhere to the specific formatting and grammar guidelines of the target magazine or competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While many choices are up to the writer, common formatting includes one-inch margins, double spacing, and 0.5" paragraph indents. Always check the venue’s rules so judges focus on story rather than formatting issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread and use grammar tools judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Polish spelling and grammar to avoid distracting errors, but vet automated suggestions carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spell checkers and grammar tools to professionalize your piece, but review each suggestion critically—software can misinterpret sentence structure and propose harmful edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely and analyze exemplary flash fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve craft by reading strong flash fiction (including past winners) and analyzing what works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take notes answering: What compelled you and why? What didn’t? How many scenes/settings/characters/side plots? How were sentences and dialogue structured? What details reveal protagonist? What surprises exist? Emulate observed strengths in your own writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn the rules before breaking them intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Know standard techniques and constraints before deliberately violating them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that rules exist for a reason; deliberate, informed rule-breaking is more effective than accidental flouting of craft principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a writer community and get feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Grow as a writer by connecting with peers to exchange ideas and feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use forums (e.g., NYC Midnight forum) to bounce ideas, ask questions, and get critique. Seek peer insight for issues not covered in the guide or when you want targeted feedback.
